# Where we left off

## Conjunctive Normal Form {.smaller}

An **AND of clauses**. Every expression has one...

::: {.fillable}
| Expression | Law |
|---|:--|
| $\neg(p \rightarrow q) \vee r$ | |
| | |
| | |
| | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[65,35]"}
:::

::: notes
  ~(p -> q) v r
  ~(~p v q) v r        IMP
  (p ^ ~q) v r         DM, then DNEG
  (p v r) ^ (~q v r)   DIST     <- CNF, two clauses

Verified: all four rows agree on all eight assignments.

:::

## Back to Inference {.smaller}

**Where we started:** Given statements (premises), a conclusion, and ten(ish) rules.
Pick a rule, pick what to apply it to, repeat until conclusion.

::: {.inference}
- $p \rightarrow q$
- $p$
- $q$
:::

**So why is that hard to hand to a machine?** 

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

\

With CNF we only need ELIM.


::: notes
Ten is a small number, so the rule count is not the problem -- push back if
someone says it is. The cost is the SEARCH:

  - at every step you choose a rule AND which of your facts to feed it, so the
    branching is the rules times the subsets, not just the rules;
  - each rule wants a different shape, so every choice needs a pattern match
    before you even know whether it applies;
  - GEN makes the space infinite on its own -- from p you may write p v q for
    ANY q, so there are always infinitely many legal next moves;
  - and nothing tells you which branch reaches the goal. You cannot tell a
    promising line from a dead one until you are down it.

That is what CNF buys. One shape, so no matching. One rule, so no choosing.
And because resolution returns what it consumes, you can apply it blindly to
every pair and stop when nothing new appears -- no cleverness anywhere.

Second blank: unit clause. Wednesday is unit propagation -- given (X) and
(~X v Y), drop ~X and keep Y. That is DS, which they have had since Friday
under the name ELIM. Do not say so now; let them find it Wednesday.
:::

# Proving by refuting

## The Trick {.smaller}

To show a conclusion **follows**, show that denying it is **impossible**.

\

::: {.fillable}
| Saying it this way | is saying |
|---|:-:|
| the conclusion follows from the premises | |
| premises $\rightarrow$ conclusion is a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ | |
| $\neg($premises $\rightarrow$ conclusion$)$ is a \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ | |
| premises $\wedge\ \neg$conclusion is \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ | |
: {tbl-colwidths="[78,22]"}
:::

::: notes
tautology / contradiction / unsatisfiable -- three ways of saying one thing,
and the last is the one a machine can hunt for.

So the recipe: negate the goal, add it to the premises, put everything in CNF,
and look for the empty clause.
:::

## Negating the Whole Thing {.smaller}

Three premises and a conclusion is one formula. We want it to be a tautology,
so we negate it and hope for a contradiction.

$$\neg\big((A \wedge B \wedge C) \rightarrow D\big)$$

::: {.fillable}
| Expression | Law |
|---|:--|
| $\neg\big(\neg(A \wedge B \wedge C) \vee D\big)$ | |
| | |
| | |
:::

\

So the premises survive untouched and **only the conclusion flips**.

::: notes
  ~((A^B^C) -> D)
  ~(~(A^B^C) v D)      IMP
  ~~(A^B^C) ^ ~D       DM
  (A^B^C) ^ ~D         DNEG   (then ASS to drop the brackets)

Verified: all five lines agree on all 16 rows.

THE POINT. This is why the recipe is "keep the premises, negate the goal" --
it is not a convention, it falls out of the algebra. Negating an implication
never touches the antecedent.

And look at the CNF: A ^ B ^ C ^ ~D is already a conjunction of FOUR UNIT
CLAUSES, {A} {B} {C} {~D}. Every premise arrives as fuel. That is why these
problems start so easily, and it is worth pointing at before the worksheet,
where some sets deliberately do not.
:::

## One Rule, Repeated

You know $(X)$. You also have $(\neg X \vee Y)$.

\

$\neg X$ is false, so it cannot be what makes that clause true. Strike it.

\

What is left must be true: \_\_\_\_\_\_

\

::: notes
Y. And they have known this rule since Friday -- it is ELIM on the Sheet,
disjunctive syllogism. The only new thing is doing it relentlessly instead of
choosing it.

This is unit propagation.
:::

## The Loop {.smaller}

Repeat until you cannot:

1. Find a clause with **exactly one literal**. It must be true. Circle it.
2. Cross out every clause that **contains** it --- satisfied, gone.
3. In every clause containing its **negation**, strike out that literal only.
4. A clause that loses its **last** literal is **$\bot$**.

\

Three ways to stop, and all three are answers:

| Stop | Means |
|---|---|
| you reach $\bot$ | the clauses contradict --- the conclusion follows |
| no clauses left | all settled, consistently --- it does **not** follow |
| clauses remain, none is a single literal | nothing more is forced |
: {tbl-colwidths="[40,60]"}

## Your Turn {.activity}

Every group has a **different** set. Annotate the sheet.

\

Answer two questions:

* What can you conclude?
* How do you know you are finished?

{{< countdown minutes=12 >}}

::: notes
13 sets, in activities/lecture-07_activity.qmd. Five reach BOTTOM, four run
out, four stall -- so all three endings are in the room, which is the debrief.

ANSWER KEY -- units in forced order:

  Set  1  -A => -E => C => F             CONTRADICTION
  Set  2  -B => D => A => G              CONTRADICTION
  Set  3  D => C => F => A               CONTRADICTION
  Set  4  G => -B => D => F              CONTRADICTION
  Set  5  C => -A => B => D              CONTRADICTION
  Set  6  B => C => F => -A => E => D    RUNS OUT
  Set  7  -G => C => D => -E => F => -B  RUNS OUT
  Set  8  -A => -D => C => B => -G => E  RUNS OUT
  Set  9  -A => D => -C => E => -B => -F RUNS OUT
  Set 10  C => F => -G => D              STALLS
  Set 11  B => -C => -D => -F            STALLS
  Set 12  -E => -F => B => -G            STALLS
  Set 13  F => -E => -A => -B            STALLS

Every sequence is forced, so a group that gets a different one has made an
error. The usual slip is a 3- or 4-literal clause: it only becomes a unit once
two or three of its literals are dead, and it is easy to treat it like the
two-literal ones.
:::

## What Did You Get? {.smaller}

::: {.fillable}
| Your ending | What it proves |
|---|---|
| $\bot$ | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| no clauses left | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
| stalled | \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ |
: {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}
:::

::: notes
BOTTOM: the premises plus the negated goal cannot all hold, so the argument is
valid. Proved.

NO CLAUSES LEFT: satisfiable, so there IS a way to make the premises true and
the conclusion false. Invalid -- and the units they derived ARE the
counterexample. Verified: in all four such sets the derived units satisfy every
clause, whichever way the one free variable goes. Ask a group to read theirs
out; it is a witness, not just a failure.

STALLED: proves nothing either way. All four stalling sets are satisfiable --
two assignments each -- so there was something to find and propagation could
not find it.

That asymmetry is the point of the whole lecture. Reaching bottom proves
validity. NOT reaching it proves nothing, unless you also ran out of clauses.
:::

## When Nothing Is Forced

$$(A\vee B)\ \wedge\ (A \vee \neg B)\ \wedge\ (\neg A \vee B)\ \wedge\ (\neg A \vee \neg B)$$

\

No clause has a single literal. The loop cannot even start.

\

And yet: is there any assignment that satisfies all four? \_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
No -- it is unsatisfiable, and all four rows of the table fail. So the answer
is THERE, propagation just cannot reach it.

What would? Pick a variable and try it both ways. Assume A: clauses 3 and 4
give B and ~B. Assume ~A: clauses 1 and 2 give B and ~B. Both branches die, so
it is unsatisfiable.

That case split is where a real SAT solver spends its life, and it is the
honest limit of what we did today.
:::

## Words and Ideas

Refutation

Unit clause, unit propagation

The empty clause $\bot$

Satisfiable, unsatisfiable

Case split
